Modern.brandNameRationale: One word. Direct. Skincare is full of promises. We named the brand after the thing customers actually want: proof. Works as a noun, works as a claim, works on a bottle in a single line.
Modern.industrySummary: Skincare has gotten loud. Every brand promises clinical, glass-skin results. Customers are smart now. They read ingredient lists. They check trial data. The category is asking for honesty more than novelty.
Modern.competitorLandscape: The Ordinary (theordinary.com) set the modern transparent template. Glossier (glossier.com) owns the cultural side. Drunk Elephant (drunkelephant.com) sits at the science-meets-design intersection. We sit closer to The Ordinary in tone, with a smaller, sharper line.
Modern.positioningRationale: Most brands sell results without showing how they got there. We publish the clinical data, the ingredient percentages, and the price reasoning on every bottle. Customers who care about skincare care about this.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Already uses three products in their routine. Reads the back of the bottle before they buy. Trusts science, not influencers. Asks questions when something doesn't work.

dos: Name the active ingredient and the percentage
donts: Photograph the founder with the bottle

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. PROOF in a precise modern grotesk, slightly compressed, all caps. The two O's set tightly together, almost touching. The mark works at every size, from a 6mm seal on a bottle to a window display.

colorPalette.name: Clinical White
colorPalette.meaning: The color of a lab notebook on a clean desk.

colorPalette.name: Lab Black
colorPalette.meaning: Ink. The wordmark. The serial number.

colorPalette.name: Test Strip Blue
colorPalette.meaning: Lab test paper. The single accent.
colorPalette.usage: Active ingredient flags, percentages on label

typography.primary: GT America Mono for label data and percentages
typography.secondary: GT America for headlines and the wordmark
typography.rationale: The mono carries the facts (ingredient percentages, batch numbers, pH). The regular carries the brand. One family, two jobs.

customSections.title: What it doesn't say
customSections.body: No miracle claims. No before-and-after photos. No celebrity endorsements. No 'natural' or 'clean beauty' language.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Bottles are clinical white with a small black wordmark. The label is a single column of data: active ingredient, percentage, pH, batch, expiry. The website shows the trial data above the buy button.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Aubade is a French word for a morning song. It's the music played as light first enters the room. We named the brand after the first ritual of the day, not the product. The word sounds like the act of waking up gently.
Luxury.story: Aubade began with a single oil, made in a Provence kitchen, for a friend who had spent a hard winter. We made twelve bottles. Then we made twelve more. Then a small atelier. The brand has grown the way the morning grows. Slowly and deliberately.
Luxury.industrySummary: The luxury end of skincare has been chasing celebrity, technology, and acquisitions. There is a quieter market for European craft brands that still operate like small ateliers. The customer wants story, ritual, and the sense that someone made this by hand.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Augustinus Bader (augustinusbader.com) set the science-luxury bar. Dr. Barbara Sturm (drsturm.com) carries the clinical-prestige angle. Le Labo for the Body (lelabofragrances.com) does the niche-craft thing in adjacent territory. We sit closer to a small French perfumer than to any of these.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A skincare house for people who treat their morning as the most important hour.

targetAudience.primary: 40 and up. Disposable income. Travels often. Owns three creams and uses one. Pays for things made slowly. Doesn't post the bottle online.

dos: Name the ingredients in their botanical Latin
Send a paper card with every order

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark, set wide, in a high contrast classical face. A small sun-rising hallmark, two concentric arcs, used as a watermark on the bottle's back label and on paper inserts.

colorPalette.name: Provence Ivory
colorPalette.meaning: Linen at dawn. Hand-laid paper. The color of restraint.

colorPalette.name: Morning Gold
colorPalette.meaning: First light on stone. Aged brass.
colorPalette.usage: Foil applications, wordmark on light surfaces

colorPalette.name: Night Indigo
colorPalette.meaning: The blue just before dawn. Anchor.

colorPalette.name: Field Sage
colorPalette.meaning: The garden the oil came from.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and primary type
typography.secondary: Söhne for the website and customer correspondence
typography.rationale: A high contrast serif carries the brand. A modern grotesk handles the digital surfaces. Each does its job and stays quiet.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No celebrity endorsements. No influencer seeding. No mass retail. No subscription model. No app.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word, two readings. The frequency (every day) and the most basic name for the practice (the daily). The brand is named after when you use it, not what's in it.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most skincare brands sell newness. New ingredient, new launch, new step. There's an opening for a brand that sells the same three things forever, and gets them right.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: The Ordinary, CeraVe (cerave.com), and basic-skincare drugstore lines occupy this space functionally but not brand-wise. We are the design-minded version of the same idea.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Three products. One routine. Replaced only when something stops working.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who don't want to think about skincare. They want it to work, to be affordable, and to never change. They buy a refill, not an upgrade.

dos: Name the function, not the ingredient
Tell customers when to stop using it

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. DAILY set in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps. The three products carry the wordmark and nothing else. Each bottle differs only by the step number: 01, 02, 03.

typography.rationale: One face. The label has the wordmark, the step number, the function, and the ingredients. Nothing else.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No serums. No masks. No oils. No limited editions. No seasonal launches. Three steps, forever.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Helix points to science without trying too hard. Dermal closes it as a category. The pair reads as a real medical-grade brand. The kind of name that already shows up on a dermatologist's invoice.
Corporate.industrySummary: Professional skincare, sold through dermatologists, med spas, and licensed estheticians, is a quiet B2B category. The buyers care about clinical efficacy, regulatory documentation, and reliable supply. Brand has been an afterthought for most players.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: SkinCeuticals (skinceuticals.com) is the standard. Obagi (obagi.com) sits beside it. ZO Skin Health (zoskinhealth.com) is the clinical-prestige peer. We compete on documentation, design, and being easier to work with than any of them.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Clinical-grade skincare distributed exclusively through licensed providers.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Practitioners need brands that hold up to dermatology questions and reorder cleanly. Helix Dermal is built around the practitioner relationship, not the consumer one.

targetAudience.primary: Dermatologists, plastic surgeons, med spa owners, licensed estheticians. They buy on documentation, reorder on reliability, and recommend to patients on outcomes.
motivations: A brand patients trust on a doctor's shelf

dos: Lead with the active and the percentage
Speak to the practitioner, not the patient

messagingPillars.name: Clinical documentation
messagingPillars.description: Every product launched with peer-reviewed trial data and complete ingredient transparency.

messagingPillars.name: Reliable distribution
messagingPillars.description: Practitioner accounts get next-day reordering and dedicated account management.

messagingPillars.name: Practitioner exclusive
messagingPillars.description: Never sold to consumers without a provider relationship.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is a single helix pattern reduced to two crossing strokes. Reads as scientific without being cartoonish. Works on practitioner packaging, professional samples, and clinical literature.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and product UI
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed clinical literature
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital and practitioner communications. The serif handles printed clinical documentation.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No D2C website. No celebrity partnerships. No influencer seeding. No retail availability. Practitioner channel only.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Glow Up is internet slang for becoming your better self. The phrase is already in the customer's vocabulary. We named the brand after the language people already use about themselves. Two words, all caps, looks great on a tube.
Creative.manifesto: Most skincare brands sound like a dermatologist trying to be your friend. We sound like your friend who already happens to know things about skincare. The product is serious. The brand is fun. The customer gets both.
Creative.industrySummary: Skincare branding has been quiet, clinical, and minimal for the last few years. The category swung clean. There's room for one that's loud, playful, fun to buy, and still backed by real formulation work.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Glossier (glossier.com) was loud and got quiet. Topicals (topicals.com) is the closest match in voice. Bubble (bubbleskincare.com) goes younger and brighter. Saie (saiehello.com) sits in the warm middle. We are louder than Saie and a bit older than Bubble.
Creative.positioningStatement: Skincare for people who want results and don't want to be bored about it.

targetAudience.primary: 20s and early 30s. Lives online. Owns more than five tubes. Buys based on packaging. Posts to close friends only. Wants the formula to work but won't read the back of the bottle.

dos: Talk to the customer like a friend

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a bold display sans with a slight upward angle, like the words are rising. The U in UP can extend a curve into a smile. Standalone smile-curve icon for stickers, social profiles, and packaging seals.

typography.primary: Migra for the wordmark and big display
typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and labels
typography.rationale: Migra has personality. Neue Montreal handles the readable bits. The pair feels designed and fun.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not clinical. Not minimal. Not afraid of pink. Not too cool to make a joke about itself.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Tubes that look great in a fridge or a flatlay. Stickers in every order. A monthly email written like a group text. Pop-up shops with mirror selfies as the marketing. A merch line that's actually good.
